about: The French course after Unit 12: every unit, lesson, guide, reading, practice set and exam through B1, with every word and pattern each one teaches. Module stubs, writer briefs, the readable plan and the course page are made from this file (scripts/plan). Positions, word counts and where each level is reached are computed, never stored. No frequency value or rank is stored here.

units.title: Joining sentences
units.can_do: You can show a newcomer round your neighbourhood: who lives where, when places open, what you like there, and what you will do if it rains.

cast: Léa, 15, the narrator, who turns 16 at the end of the unit; lives on the third floor of a building in the Croix-Rousse, a hillside neighbourhood of Lyon
Noé, 9, her brother
their mother (maman), a nurse who works nights
Maya, 15, who has just moved from Montréal into the flat above and knows nobody yet
Hugo, 16, Léa's best friend since primary school; sings badly and loves it
Mme Garnier, 78, on the ground floor, a retired teacher who has lived in the building for fifty years
Karim, about 45, the baker on their street (met here, central in Unit 14)
places: Léa's building and its stairs
Karim's bakery
the library
the swimming pool
the Sunday market
the park above the river
Léa's flat on the night of her party
situations: pointing out the people in the building and the street to a newcomer
walking a newcomer round the neighbourhood and saying what happens where
saying when the bakery, the library and the pool open and close, and dropping by a friend's flat
making Saturday plans that depend on the weather
inviting friends to a birthday party, accepting or refusing, and thanking
introducing people at the party, singing and dancing

culture.customs: bonjour on the stairs; tu and vous with neighbours; the small words of speech and the short forms people say

units.sound: nasal [ɛ̃] that opens into a heard n: voisin / voisine, copain / copine; que shortens before a vowel (qu'il, qu'elle) and qui never does

modules.title: {qui} and {que} after a noun (le voisin qui parle, le livre que je lis)
modules.goal: You can say which person or thing you mean by what it does or what someone does to it: le monsieur qui habite à côté, le livre que je lis.
modules.situation: Opens with Léa and Maya at the window, Léa pointing out the people in the street; closes with Maya naming them back: la voisine qui a un chien, le copain que tu cherches.
modules.spoken_example: C'est qui, le mec qui parle à Karim ? C'est quoi, le truc que tu cherches ?
modules.note: lire gets a full present table (lis, lit, lisons, lisez, lisent) and its participle lu; préfère, achète and sort are glossed forms of taught verbs.

modules.title: {où} after a place or a time (la bibliothèque où je travaille, le jour où Maya est arrivée)
modules.goal: You can name a place or a day by what happens there: la piscine où Noé nage, le jour où Maya est arrivée.
modules.situation: Opens on the stairs as Léa offers to show Maya round; closes at the top of the street with Maya saying where she will go first.
modules.culture_note: In a French building you say bonjour to every neighbour you pass on the stairs, even one you have never met. Walking past in silence is what counts as rude.
modules.spoken_example: Euh… on va où, d'abord ? — Ben, à la boulangerie. C'est là où je vais tous les matins, hein.
modules.note: marché gets its own noun card so the checker reads it as the noun, not the participle of marcher.

modules.title: Opening hours and errands ({ouvrir}, {fermer}, {passer}, {oublier})
modules.goal: You can say when a place opens and closes, that you will drop by, and what someone forgot: La boulangerie ouvre à sept heures. Je passe chez toi ce soir.
modules.situation: Opens with Maya reading the bakery's opening hours on the door; closes with Maya locked out because she forgot her key, and Léa passing by.
modules.spoken_example: Ouais, j'ai oublié ma clé. Bref, je peux pas entrer.
modules.note: ouvrir needs a table of its irregular forms (ouvre, ouvres, ouvrons, ouvrez, ouvrent; participle ouvert). Reuses où and qui with the places of the last lesson.

modules.title: {si} + present: plans that depend on something (s'il pleut, on va à la bibliothèque)
modules.goal: You can make a plan that depends on the weather or on someone: S'il fait beau, on prend les vélos. Si tu veux, on y va.
modules.situation: Opens with Léa and Hugo reading the weather forecast for Saturday; closes with three plans, one for sun, one for rain, one for snow.
modules.spoken_example: S'il pleut, on va à la bibliothèque ? — Bof.
modules.note: neiger moves here from Unit 14 (il neige, s'il neige); the graph needs its present form neige.

modules.title: {ce que} and {ce qui}: saying what (ce que j'aime, ce qui est drôle)
modules.goal: You can say what you like, what is important and what is hard without naming the thing first: Ce que j'aime surtout, c'est le marché. Ce qui est drôle, c'est Hugo.
modules.situation: Opens with Maya asking what there is to do here; closes with Léa's list of favourite things and Maya saying what she loved in Montréal.
modules.spoken_example: Ce que j'aime ici, en fait, c'est le marché. Il y a, genre, dix boulangeries.

modules.title: An invitation ({inviter}, {accepter}, {refuser}, {remercier})
modules.goal: You can invite someone, accept or refuse politely, and thank them: Je t'invite à mon anniversaire samedi. Merci, j'accepte avec plaisir.
modules.situation: Opens with Léa writing invitations for her sixteenth birthday; closes with the answers: Hugo accepts, Mme Garnier refuses kindly, Maya has not answered yet.
modules.spoken_example: Maya n'a pas répondu. Du coup, je sais pas si elle vient.
modules.note: anniversaire and fête are open in the Reference unit; cadeau is taught by its first-use fix in Unit 11 (donner).

modules.title: {dont}: the one you talk about (le quartier dont je suis fière)
modules.goal: You can describe someone or something by what you say or feel about it: le garçon dont je t'ai parlé, un quartier dont je suis fière.
modules.situation: Opens with Mme Garnier showing Léa old photos of the street; closes with Léa telling Maya about the people Mme Garnier talked about.
modules.culture_note: Léa says vous to Mme Garnier and tu to Maya. An adult neighbour gets vous until she offers tu; someone your own age gets tu from the first word.
modules.spoken_example: C'est Hugo, le pote dont je t'ai parlé, tu vois ?
modules.note: fier is carded with fière; the adj.er pattern is not taught, so other -er feminines are glossed. The Unit 10 practice set names dont on a concept card: take it off there.

modules.title: Which relative? ({qui}, {que}, {où}, {dont}, {ce qui}, {ce que})
modules.goal: Puts the five relatives in one table: what comes after the noun (a verb, a subject, a place or time, de) picks the word. Builds on the Unit 12 guide Who and What Questions, which already splits qui (does the action) from que (receives it).

modules.title: The party ({présenter}, {chanter}, {danser}, {détester})
modules.goal: You can introduce people and say what you love or hate doing at a party: Je te présente Maya. Hugo chante, mais je déteste danser.
modules.situation: Opens as the guests arrive at Léa's flat; closes with everyone singing Joyeux anniversaire and Maya dancing with Noé.
modules.spoken_example: Franchement, tu danses trop bien !
modules.note: The reading that follows reuses all four verbs, inside the two-module reuse window.

modules.title: How people really talk ({euh}, {ben}, {hein}, {quoi}, {en fait}, {du coup}, {genre}, {bref})
modules.goal: Gathers the small words French speakers use to think aloud, soften what they say and react, as English speakers say um, like and you know. To hesitate: euh, ben, bah. To start or close: bon, alors, voilà, enfin, bref. To check the listener is following: hein, tu vois, and quoi at the end of a sentence. To explain: en fait, du coup. To react: ouais, bof, franchement, genre. Then the short forms of fast speech, which the learner hears from the first day: ne dropped (je sais pas), on for nous, tu cut short before a vowel (t'as, t'es), il y a said y'a and je ne sais pas said chais pas. The learner uses the small words and understands the short forms. In writing, ne and the full forms stay.

reading.genre: a guide written as a letter, second person
reading.premise: Maya, fifteen, has just moved from Montréal into the flat above Léa's in the Croix-Rousse, and she knows nobody. Léa writes her a guide to the neighbourhood and slips it under her door: Karim's bakery, which opens at seven, the library where Léa does her homework, the market whose cheese seller knows everyone, and Mme Garnier on the ground floor, a neighbour Léa is proud of. Because Maya comes from Québec, Léa also explains what is done here: you say bonjour to every neighbour you pass on the stairs, you say vous to Mme Garnier until she tells you otherwise, and the meal Maya calls souper is called dîner. Each place comes with a plan for the weather: if it rains, the library; if it is sunny, bikes along the river; if it snows, hot chocolate at Mme Garnier's. The guide ends with an invitation to Léa's birthday party on Saturday, where Hugo will sing and everyone will dance, and under it a short reply in Maya's handwriting: she accepts, and asks what she should bring.
reading.questions: match each place or person to the relative clause that describes it; which plan goes with which weather; what Maya is invited to and what she answers; what Léa tells Maya about manners in the building

modules.title: Practice · Joining sentences
modules.summary: About 20 items, grouped by goal and interleaved: join two sentences with the right relative, gap-fill qui/que/où/dont/ce qui/ce que, si-plans from a weather forecast, opening hours, and invitation replies.

units.title: Verbs at work
units.can_do: You can serve customers at a counter, take an order on the phone and run a shop for an hour, and say what you did at work each day.

cast: Léa, 16, on her first summer job, one week in July
Karim, about 45, the baker who owns the bakery on Léa's street; patient, precise, grew up in the neighbourhood
Noé, 9, her brother, whom she takes to the pool before work
Mme Garnier, the neighbour from Unit 13, a customer every morning
Maya and Hugo, who drop in
customers: a man ordering a birthday cake for his wife, a woman who phones in an order, a father with a small boy
places: Karim's bakery: the counter, the shelves, the till, the phone
the street and the square Léa crosses at six in the morning
the pool where she leaves Noé
situations: learning the work on the first morning: filling shelves, customers choosing
selling, answering questions and giving change
getting ready and getting to work early
serving customers with the polite formulas of a shop
taking a birthday-cake order and writing the message on it
taking and confirming an order on the phone, spelling a name
running the shop alone for an hour

culture.customs: bonjour in a shop; daily bread and the baguette; the 14th of July

units.sound: the consonant heard only in the plural: il choisit / ils choisissent, il vend / ils vendent, il répond / ils répondent; é in the infinitive, è where the ending is silent: répéter / je répète, espérer / j'espère

modules.title: -ir verbs like {finir} (je choisis, nous choisissons)
modules.goal: You can use any regular -ir verb in the present, the past, after il faut que and with en: Elle choisit un gâteau. J'ai rempli les sacs. Il faut que je choisisse. En réfléchissant…
modules.situation: Opens at six on Monday as Karim shows Léa the shelves to fill; closes with the first customers choosing and Karim saying he grew up on this street.
modules.culture_note: Most French households buy fresh bread every day, and a neighbourhood is judged by its bakery. In 2022 UNESCO added the craft and culture of the baguette to its heritage list.
modules.spoken_example: Alors, le boulot, ça te plaît ?
modules.note: finir is the model (already taught). The learner already knows the passé composé, the subjunctive triggers and en + -ant with -er verbs, so the lesson maps each onto -ir.

modules.title: -re verbs like {attendre} (je réponds, nous répondons)
modules.goal: You can use any regular -re verb in the present, the past, after il faut que and with en: Je vends du pain. Elle a répondu. Je vous rends deux euros.
modules.situation: Opens with Léa behind the counter for the first time; closes with her giving change and answering a customer she did not hear the first time.
modules.spoken_example: A customer mumbles. Léa says Pardon ? and not Hein ?, which is too abrupt behind a counter.
modules.note: attendre, rendre, perdre and descendre are already taught and become examples of the pattern. entendre is taught here; its first-use fix sits in the Unit 9 practice set, which teaches nothing, so that sentence needs a gloss or a rewrite.

modules.title: Before work ({se doucher}, {porter}, {traverser}, {emmener})
modules.goal: You can say how you get ready and get somewhere early, and whom you take with you: Je me douche à six heures, je traverse la place et j'emmène Noé à la piscine.
modules.situation: Opens with Léa's alarm on Tuesday; closes at the bakery door at seven, carrying the croissants Karim asked her to bring to Mme Garnier.
modules.spoken_example: Je bosse à sept heures. — Ouais, c'est tôt.
modules.note: emmener has the è spelling change (j'emmène); porter needs its present and participle forms in the graph.

modules.title: Serving at the counter ({désirer}, {servir}, {tenir}, {garder}, {prier}, {toucher})
modules.goal: You can serve a customer from greeting to goodbye: Bonjour madame, vous désirez ? Je vous sers une baguette ? Tenez. Je vous en prie.
modules.situation: Opens with Mme Garnier's morning order; closes with a small boy touching every cake in the window and Léa asking him, kindly, to stop.
modules.culture_note: A customer says bonjour on entering a French shop, before asking for anything, and au revoir on leaving. Bonjour comes first even when the queue is long.
modules.note: tenir (tiens, tenons, tiennent, tenu) and servir (sers, servons, servent, servi) get tables; prier is taught in je vous en prie and je t'en prie; garder needs its present and participle forms in the graph.

modules.title: A birthday cake ({offrir}, {écrire}, {dessiner}, {souhaiter}, {espérer}, {féliciter})
modules.goal: You can take an order for a gift and wish someone well: Je voudrais offrir un gâteau à ma femme. Vous pouvez écrire « Bon anniversaire » ? J'espère qu'elle va aimer.
modules.situation: Opens with a man ordering a cake for his wife's birthday; closes with Léa writing the message and drawing a flower on it, and Karim congratulating her.
modules.note: offrir (offre, offrons, offert) and écrire (écris, écrivons, écrit) get tables; espérer has the è change. souhaiter and espérer are set side by side: souhaiter + noun or que, espérer + que + indicative.

modules.title: Verb patterns, part 2 (-er, -ir and -re side by side; the irregular verbs that follow -ir or -re)
modules.goal: Sets the three groups side by side in the present and the participle, then the irregular verbs that keep one group's endings: partir, sortir, dormir and servir (-ir with no -iss-), ouvrir and offrir (-ir verbs with -er endings), prendre and mettre (-re with their own stems). Follows the Unit 3 guide Understanding Verb Patterns.

modules.title: Orders by phone ({téléphoner}, {réserver}, {confirmer}, {rappeler}, {répéter}, {épeler})
modules.goal: You can take an order on the phone, ask the caller to repeat or spell, and promise to call back: Allô ? Vous pouvez répéter ? Vous pouvez épeler votre nom ? Je vous rappelle pour confirmer.
modules.situation: Opens with the phone ringing while Karim is in the back; closes with Léa calling the customer back to confirm two cakes for Saturday.
modules.note: allô moves here from Unit 16. rappeler, répéter and épeler have spelling changes (rappelle, répète, épelle); téléphoner needs its present and participle forms in the graph.

modules.title: Spelling changes in -er verbs (j'achète, je répète, j'appelle, nous mangeons)
modules.goal: Gathers the -er verbs whose stem changes where the ending is silent: è (acheter, lever, préférer, emmener, espérer, répéter), a double consonant (appeler, rappeler, épeler, jeter) and nous mangeons, nous commençons. The learner has met these in Units 5 to 14 as separate forms; the guide shows they follow one sound rule.

modules.title: In charge for an hour ({s'occuper de}, {laisser}, {envoyer}, {quitter}, {arrêter})
modules.goal: You can take charge when someone leaves and report what happened: Karim m'a laissé le magasin. Je me suis occupée des clients et je lui ai envoyé une photo.
modules.situation: Opens on Friday as Karim leaves for an hour and gives Léa instructions; closes with Karim back and Léa telling him what she did.
modules.culture_note: Léa's week falls in July, the month of the national holiday. On the 14th there are fireworks in every town, and many fire stations hold a public dance the night before.
modules.spoken_example: Un monsieur est passé, une dame a téléphoné… Bref, tout va bien.
modules.note: envoyer has the y/i change (envoie, envoyons); occuper needs its present and participle forms in the graph.

reading.genre: a dialogue-led story in six short scenes, Monday to Saturday, third person
reading.premise: In July, Léa works her first summer job: a week at Karim's bakery on her street. On Monday she fills the shelves and learns what each regular chooses; on Tuesday a customer on the phone has to spell her name twice; on Wednesday a man orders a cake for his wife, and Léa writes the message on it herself. On Thursday a small boy touches every cake in the window while his father waits for his change, and on Friday Karim leaves Léa alone with the shop for an hour, which goes better than either of them expected. On Saturday Karim congratulates her, pays her for the week and gives her a cake to take to her cousin's wedding in Saint-Malo, and asks whether she will come back next summer.
reading.questions: what Léa did on each day; what each customer chose or ordered; who says which shop formula; why Karim congratulates her and what he gives her

units.title: Looking back and ahead
units.can_do: You can tell the story of a trip: what had already happened when you arrived, what would have happened if, what was built by whom, and what will be done by the time you get home.

cast: Léa, 16, keeping a diary of the trip
Noé, 9, her brother, who breaks things and tells stories
their mother (maman), who worries about trains
Camille, 28, their cousin, who marries Julien in Saint-Malo
Julien, 30, her husband
Yann, Camille's father, Léa's uncle, who lives in Saint-Malo and drives everyone around
Hugo, back in Lyon, whom Léa misses
places: the train from Lyon and the connection at Rennes
Yann's car
the wedding and the meal in a hotel by the sea
the walled old town of Saint-Malo, its beach and port
situations: packing and regretting what you should have done
a late train: what would have happened if
being met at the station and driven
arriving when things had already happened
the wedding ceremony
the wedding meal: bringing and receiving gifts, photos
planning the last days and the return home
visiting old buildings: who built them, when
something broken, and who did it

culture.history: Saint-Malo's medieval walls and the town rebuilt after 1944

units.sound: aurai or aurais, serai or serais: in careful speech the closed é of the future against the open è of the conditional, which tells the future perfect from the past conditional by ear

modules.title: Past conditional with {avoir} (j'aurais dû, tu aurais pu)
modules.goal: You can say what you should have done, could have done or would have liked: J'aurais dû préparer ma valise hier. Tu aurais pu me le dire !
modules.situation: Opens at six in the morning with Léa's half-packed suitcase and the tickets nowhere; closes on the train, listing what each of them should have done.
modules.spoken_example: T'aurais dû prendre du fric pour le taxi.

modules.title: Past conditional with {être} (je serais venue, nous serions arrivés)
modules.goal: You can say what would have happened with the être verbs: Si le train était parti à l'heure, nous serions arrivés à trois heures. Si tu n'étais pas venue, je serais restée à Lyon.
modules.situation: Opens with the train stopped outside Rennes; closes on the platform as the connection waits and maman lists what would have happened if it had not.

modules.title: Getting there ({conduire}, {amener}, {manquer}, {s'inquiéter})
modules.goal: You can talk about being driven and brought, missing a train or a person, and worrying: Mon oncle conduit, il nous amène à l'hôtel. Ne t'inquiète pas. Hugo me manque.
modules.situation: Opens with Yann waiting at Rennes station; closes in the car on the coast road, Léa texting Hugo that she misses him.
modules.spoken_example: Montez, c'est ma vieille bagnole. Léa to Hugo, by text: tkt, on arrive.
modules.note: oncle is carded here, where Yann first appears. conduire gets a table (conduis, conduisons, conduit); amener and inquiéter have the è change; manquer is taught in both senses (manquer le train, tu me manques).

modules.title: Three kinds of if ({si} + present, {si} + imparfait, {si} + plus-que-parfait)
modules.goal: Lines up the three si sentences by how real they are: a real plan (si tu veux, on y va), a daydream (si j'étais riche, je voyagerais), a past that did not happen (si j'avais su, je serais venue). Placed after both past-conditional lessons so the third kind is shown in full, with both helpers.

modules.title: Pluperfect with {être} (elle était déjà partie)
modules.goal: You can say what had already happened when you arrived, with the être verbs: Quand nous sommes arrivés, Camille était déjà partie et mon oncle était allé à la gare.
modules.situation: Opens at the hotel the evening before the wedding; closes with Léa piecing together what had happened before they arrived.

modules.title: The wedding ({se marier}, {promettre}, {pleurer}, {jeter})
modules.goal: You can describe a ceremony: who marries, what they promise, who cries, what is thrown: Camille et Julien se marient. Ils se promettent… Tout le monde pleure.
modules.situation: Opens as the guests take their seats; closes with Camille throwing her flowers and Léa catching them.
modules.culture_note: A French marriage is made at the town hall, in front of the mayor or a deputy, and that ceremony is the legal one. A religious wedding, if there is one, comes after it.
modules.note: promettre follows mettre (promets, promis); jeter doubles its t (je jette); marier needs its present and participle forms in the graph.

modules.title: The wedding meal ({recevoir}, {imaginer}, {bouger}, with {apporter})
modules.goal: You can say who brought what, who received what, and ask the guests to keep still for a photo: Nous avons apporté le gâteau de Karim. Les mariés ont reçu beaucoup de cadeaux. Ne bougez pas !
modules.situation: Opens with Léa carrying Karim's cake into the hotel; closes with the family photo and Noé unable to keep still.
modules.spoken_example: Noé: On bouffe quand ? — Maman: On dit « on mange quand », Noé.
modules.note: apporter is already taught (Reading 5 table, position 68), so the plan's Unit 15 copy is dropped and the lesson reuses it; invité moves here from Unit 18. recevoir gets a table (reçois, recevons, reçoivent, reçu: the ç before o and u); bouger keeps its e before o (nous bougeons).

modules.title: Future perfect (quand nous serons rentrés, j'aurai fini)
modules.goal: You can say what will be done by a time in the future: Quand nous serons rentrés, j'aurai fini mon journal. Dans un mois, l'école aura commencé.
modules.situation: Opens on the last morning as maman plans the return; closes with Léa writing what will have changed by the time she sees Hugo again.

modules.title: The passive (les murs ont été construits au XIIe siècle)
modules.goal: You can say what was done and by whom, when the thing done is more important than the person who did it: Ces murs ont été construits il y a huit siècles. Beaucoup de maisons ont été construites après la guerre. Le gâteau a été fait par Karim.
modules.situation: Opens on the old town walls with Yann as guide; closes back at the hotel, where Camille asks who made the cake.
modules.culture_note: Saint-Malo's walls go back to the twelfth century. Most of the old town inside them was destroyed in August 1944 and rebuilt in its old style after the war.

modules.title: Every compound tense is a helper + participle
modules.goal: One table: avoir or être in the present, imparfait, conditionnel or futur, plus the participle, gives every compound tense the course teaches; être + participle of an avoir verb is the passive. Agreement follows the same rule in every row.

modules.title: Something broken ({casser}, {enlever}, {mentir}, {raconter})
modules.goal: You can say what broke and who did it, ask for the story and spot a fib: Qui a cassé le verre ? Raconte-moi ce qui s'est passé. Tu mens !
modules.situation: Opens with a crash in the hotel breakfast room; closes with Noé telling the truth and helping pick up the pieces.
modules.note: verre moves here from Unit 16. mentir gets a table (mens, mentons, menti); enlever has the è change.

reading.genre: a diary in five dated entries, first person
reading.premise: Léa, her mother and Noé take the train from Lyon to Saint-Malo for cousin Camille's wedding, with Karim's cake on Léa's knees. Their first train runs late, and if the connection at Rennes had not waited they would have missed the wedding; when they reach the hotel, Camille and her father have already gone out. At the wedding Camille and Julien make their promises, half the guests cry, and Léa catches the flowers; the next day Yann shows them the old town, whose walls were begun about eight hundred years ago and whose streets were rebuilt after the war, while Noé breaks a glass at breakfast and lies about it, then owns up. In the last entry, on the train home, Léa writes what she should have done differently, and what will have changed by the time she is back in Lyon: school will have started, and she will have spent all her bakery money.
reading.questions: the order of events; what happened against what would have happened; what had already happened when they arrived; what was built when and by whom; what will be done by the end of the summer

units.title: A family weekend {un week-end en famille}
units.can_do: You can introduce your relatives, show someone round a house, cook a meal together, tell someone's life story, keep a secret, play a game and say where it hurts.

cast: Amélie, 8, from Reading 12
Claire and Antoine, her parents
Henri, her grandfather, a widower, who turns 80 this weekend; he lives in a village on the Normandy coast
Tante Nadia (Claire's sister), her husband Sam and their baby Rose, who fly in from Montréal
Jeanne, Antoine's mother, who comes by train; to her, Henri is family by marriage
Amélie's cousin, 12, Nadia's eldest
the village doctor, the bookseller
places: Henri's house: the entrance, the salon, the bathroom, the kitchen
the airport and the road at midnight
the village: church, post office, bookshop, crossroads, tennis court
the doctor's surgery
the hills behind the village
situations: greeting relatives at the door and saying who is who
arrivals by plane and taxi, late at night
setting the table and cooking the birthday lunch
a fall from a bike and a visit to the doctor
games after lunch and a surprise party
Henri's stories of his younger years
a secret to keep until Sunday lunch

culture.customs: la bise; the Sunday lunch from apéritif to coffee; faire le pont

units.sound: Nasal vowels in the family and food words: tante, enchanté and an; oignon and on; bain and in, as in cousin from Unit 15. Then silent final consonants in the body words: dos, nez, doigt, bras.

modules.title: The family arrives {la famille}
modules.goal: You can introduce each relative by name and say how they are related: c'est ma tante, le mari de ma tante.
modules.situation: Opens at Henri's front door as the relatives arrive and greet each other; closes with Amélie explaining the family to the taxi driver: Henri is Papa's beau-père, Rose is Tante Nadia's baby.
modules.culture_note: Family and friends greet each other with la bise, a light kiss on each cheek. How many depends on the region: two in most places, three or four in some.
modules.note: monsieur moved to Unit 13. mademoiselle: usually for a girl, and old-fashioned for a woman. neveu and nièce come from version 2.

modules.title: Getting there {le trajet}
modules.goal: You can say how you are travelling, how long it takes and when you will arrive: on arrive à minuit et quart.
modules.situation: Opens with Nadia's call from the airport in Montréal; closes with Henri waiting for the last taxi, a quarter of an hour after midnight, and the baby's seat in the back.

modules.title: Round the house {la maison}
modules.goal: You can show someone round a house and say where everyone will sleep.
modules.situation: Opens with Henri showing the rooms and their old furniture, from the entrance to the bathroom; closes with the sleeping plan: the baby in the salon, Amélie on the sofa against the wall with the sea view.

modules.title: Setting the table {la table}
modules.goal: You can set a table and ask for what is missing at breakfast or lunch.
modules.situation: Opens at breakfast, when there is no cup for Rose's bottle; closes with Amélie setting the table for twelve and saying bon appétit at noon.
modules.culture_note: A family lunch on Sunday follows a fixed order: apéritif, starter, main dish, cheese, dessert, coffee. It can last all afternoon, and everyone says bon appétit before the first mouthful.
modules.note: verre moved to Unit 15. bon appétit needs a chunk (open).

modules.title: Cooking with Grandpa {cuisiner}
modules.goal: You can follow and give the steps of a simple recipe.
modules.situation: Opens with Henri teaching Amélie his tart, with oil, cream and a slice of butter, and a smell of burning from the oven; closes with the candles counted, eighty of them, and a vote on the ice-cream flavour.

modules.title: Where does it hurt? {avoir mal à}
modules.goal: You can say where it hurts and answer a doctor's questions.
modules.situation: Opens with Amélie's cousin falling off the bike in a race down the lane; closes at the doctor's: J'ai mal au bras et au dos.
modules.note: Teaches avoir mal à + body part (mal au dos, mal aux dents) as a frame; the graph has no construction for it yet (open).

modules.title: Round the village {le village}
modules.goal: You can ask where a place is and whether it is open, and suggest a walk.
modules.situation: Opens with Amélie sent to buy Henri's paper on the public holiday; closes at the crossroads: the bookshop is open, the post office is shut, and normally Henri feels like a walk in the hills.
modules.culture_note: When a public holiday falls on a Thursday or a Tuesday, many people take off the day between it and the weekend too. The French call this faire le pont, making the bridge.

modules.title: {avoir} where English says to be
modules.goal: French uses avoir for many states English names with to be: j'ai faim, j'ai froid, tu as raison, j'ai besoin de, j'ai envie de, j'ai mal au dos. The guide puts the ones the learner owns in one table and adds the age pattern j'ai huit ans.

modules.title: Grandpa's younger years {la jeunesse d'Henri}
modules.goal: You can tell the story of someone's younger years: where they served, whom they married and how they brought up their children.
modules.situation: Opens with Henri showing Amélie a photo of himself at twenty, a soldier doing his army service in peacetime, and telling how his own father fought the enemy for the country's freedom; closes with how he met his fiancée, married her and brought up two daughters with her until her death.
modules.note: mort is taught as the noun (la mort); the adjective and the participle of mourir are forms a gloss covers. époux is formal next to mari, taught at the start of the unit.

modules.title: Games after lunch {les jeux}
modules.goal: You can suggest a game, join in and say what makes people laugh.
modules.situation: Opens after the birthday lunch, when Henri brings out his old board games and the cousins look for a ball; closes with songs, jokes and a family club for next summer.

modules.title: Keeping the secret {le secret}
modules.goal: You can promise to keep a secret, and say what someone noticed, claimed or did not know.
modules.situation: Opens with Amélie swearing to her mother that she will say nothing about the party; closes when Henri notices the extra plates, Amélie claims not to know why, and the secret nearly comes out.
modules.note: prétendre means to claim and ignorer means not to know; both are false friends for English speakers and join the Unit 19 guide's examples.

modules.title: The surprise party {la fête}
modules.goal: You can invite someone, accept, congratulate and pay a compliment.
modules.situation: Opens with the invitation Amélie draws for the party; closes with the toast: congratulations, compliments, and Henri's story of the job he did for forty years.
modules.note: d'accord comes from accord; the graph needs d'accord as a chunk (open).

reading.premise: For Henri's eightieth birthday, Claire secretly gathers the whole family at his house in Normandy over a long holiday weekend. Nadia, Sam and baby Rose land at midnight after the flight from Montréal, Jeanne arrives by train, and Amélie's job is to keep her grandfather out of the house on Saturday morning while the others cook. Her cousin falls off the bike on the way back from the village and needs the doctor, and the secret nearly comes out. At Sunday lunch the family surprises Henri with a cake, eighty candles and a song; then Henri takes out his old camera and shows them the surprise he had prepared: a photo of each of them as a baby, because he had guessed everything.

units.title: Sophie's new job {un nouveau travail}
units.can_do: You can work in a team, compare options and give advice, describe people, plan guests' travel and clothes for an evening, say that you are worried, sort out a mistake politely and say who was to blame.

cast: Sophie, about 35, from Readings 2, 3 and 10, who dreamed of a different life and has moved to Bordeaux to work for a small events agency
Bruno, the agency's director
Yanis, 26, her colleague, who jokes all day
Clara, 37, the client, who wants a reunion of her lycée class twenty years after they left school
Clara's old classmates, some married, some single, some living abroad
Mathieu, the classmate the class once accused of stealing an exam paper, single and still fond of Clara
the owner of a wine château; a caterer
places: the agency's open-plan office in Bordeaux
the château, its courtyard and cellars
the caterer's kitchen
the station and the airport

a client's story and a class photo
choosing between three venues
guests travelling from abroad, and something to wear
a tasting and nerves the night before
a printing mistake to put right and an old story of who was to blame

modules.title: First day at the agency {le bureau}
modules.goal: You can introduce yourself at work and say who does what in a team.
modules.situation: Opens at the front desk of a small events agency in Bordeaux; closes with Sophie's first job from the director on her screen: a class reunion, twenty years on.

modules.title: Old friends {l'amitié}
modules.goal: You can tell how people met and talk about love and friendship.
modules.situation: Opens as Clara, the client, shows Sophie the class photo from 2006; closes with the story of a ring that one classmate never gave.
modules.note: mariage moved to Unit 15.

modules.title: Who's who in the class photo {le caractère}
modules.goal: You can describe someone's character and say how two people differ.
modules.situation: Opens with Clara naming her classmates for the seating plan; closes with the tables: the calm ones together, the worried one near the door.
modules.note: drôle and fier moved to Units 13 to 15. bête, idiot, stupide and malheureux come from Unit 18's stub.

modules.title: Choosing a venue {le choix}
modules.goal: You can compare options, give advice and say which you prefer and why.
modules.situation: Opens with three venues on the table at the agency; closes with Clara's choice of a wine château.
modules.culture_note: Bordeaux is France's best-known wine region. A château there is a wine estate, whether or not it has a castle.

modules.title: Guests from abroad {les arrivées}
modules.goal: You can give travel details for guests and say who will meet them: flights, documents, arrival times.
modules.situation: Opens with guests flying in from Montréal, Berlin and Moscow; closes with Sophie's arrivals sheet: flight, passport, hotel, who collects whom, and a guest to warn that his flight has changed.

modules.title: Something to wear {les vêtements}
modules.goal: You can ask for a size, try something on and say whether it fits.
modules.situation: Opens with Sophie and Clara looking for something to wear for the reunion; closes with a jacket in Sophie's size and a hat Clara does not need.

modules.title: Visiting the château {la visite}
modules.goal: You can describe a place and say what is allowed and what is not.
modules.situation: Opens at the château gate with the owner; closes with the rules: no candles upstairs, no cars in the courtyard.

modules.title: Tasting the menu {la dégustation}
modules.goal: You can say how food tastes, ask for more and give your opinion of a meal.
modules.situation: Opens at the caterer's tasting with produce from a farm nearby; closes with the director tasting everything twice.

modules.title: Nerves before the big day {le trac}
modules.goal: You can say that you are worried and why, and tell someone to relax.
modules.situation: Opens with Sophie awake the night before her first event, afraid the caterer will be late; closes with Yanis telling her to relax, since nothing annoys a client more than a nervous organiser.
modules.spoken_example: Yanis: T'inquiète. Franchement, tout est prêt.

modules.title: When it goes wrong {la faute}
modules.goal: You can say whose fault something is, apologise and calm a disagreement.
modules.situation: Opens when the printed name cards come back with the wrong names; closes with an apology and a fix: unfortunately the wrong cards, fortunately new ones by Friday.
modules.note: Gathers the conflict words of the stubs talk-facon and talk-contact.

modules.title: Whose fault was it? {à qui la faute ?}
modules.goal: You can say who you think is responsible, give proof, admit a point and defend yourself.
modules.situation: Opens with Clara telling the old story of the exam paper stolen in their last year at the lycée: the class accused Mathieu, who insisted he was innocent; closes with the guilty one owning up in the class's group chat twenty years on, and Yanis playing the judge.
modules.note: défendre is taught in both senses: to defend someone and to forbid something.

modules.title: Adverbs in -ment {heureusement}
modules.goal: Most adverbs add -ment to the feminine adjective: heureux, heureuse, heureusement; lent, lente, lentement. Adjectives ending in a vowel add -ment directly: vrai, vraiment; facile, facilement. Then the ones to recognise: absolument, justement, parfaitement. Met in vraiment, seulement, rapidement, lentement, simplement, généralement (Units 1 to 12), justement, absolument, parfaitement (Choosing a venue), heureusement, malheureusement (When it goes wrong).

units.title: A week on a farm {la classe verte}
units.can_do: You can describe farm and wild animals, nature and the weather, say what a farm grows and makes, follow a class activity, say how you feel when you are ill or upset, and tell a story.

cast: Amélie, now 9, and her class
Théo, 9, her friend, who falls ill
Madame Roux, their teacher
Madame Chabrol, the farmer
the bus driver
Samir, the nurse at the holiday centre
places: the bus and the motorway
a farm in the Auvergne: barn, henhouse, yard
the woods and a lake
the dormitory
the centre's nurse's room
situations: a long bus journey
packing and checking a list
looking after animals and picking fruit and vegetables
a walk in the heat and a storm
class in the barn, a quarrel and an illness
an evening game and stories after lights out

culture.history: Vercingétorix and Gergovie; the volcanoes of the Auvergne

units.sound: ch against j and soft g: vache, cheval, cochon, chauffeur, chaîne, chaleur against genou, gorge, joue, page, général.

modules.title: The bus to the farm {l'excursion}
modules.goal: You can talk about a journey: distance, speed, delays and the time it takes.
modules.situation: Opens at seven in the morning at the school gate; closes with the driver's news: three hundred kilometres, a lorry too slow to overtake and arrival at four.

modules.title: Packing for the trip {la liste}
modules.goal: You can check a packing list and say what is needed and who is responsible for it.
modules.situation: Opens with the teacher's list the evening before; closes at the bus door as she counts the pupils.
modules.culture_note: Many French primary pupils go away with their class at least once: a classe verte in the country, a classe de neige in the mountains or a classe de mer by the sea.
modules.note: élève and the school things come from Unit 16's stub school-describing-seul, which is retired.

modules.title: Animals on the farm {les animaux}
modules.goal: You can describe animals and say what you may and may not do with them.
modules.situation: Opens with the farmer, Madame Chabrol, showing the barn; closes at dusk with the class collecting eggs and catching a hen.

modules.title: Wild animals round the farm {les bêtes sauvages}
modules.goal: You can say which animals are wild, what each one eats and what to do when one bites or stings.
modules.situation: Opens with Madame Chabrol feeding the sheep and the ducks and telling how a wolf was seen in the hills last winter, in the hunting season; closes with Théo stung by an insect, flies round the barn and a mouse under a bed in the dormitory.

modules.title: What the farm grows {le potager}
modules.goal: You can name fruit and vegetables, write a shopping list and say what goes into each dish.
modules.situation: Opens in Madame Chabrol's kitchen garden, with carrots, onions and strawberries to pick; closes with the class writing the menu for the farm lunch: onion soup, ham with potatoes, yoghurt and homemade jam.

modules.title: Forest, lake and storm {la nature}
modules.goal: You can describe weather and nature and change a plan because of a storm.
modules.situation: Opens with a walk through the woods to the lake in the heat, and the geography of the old volcanoes; closes back at the farm as the storm breaks.
modules.culture_note: The round green hills of the Auvergne are old volcanoes, about eighty of them in one line called the Chaîne des Puys. The last one erupted several thousand years ago, and the chain has been a UNESCO site since 2018.
modules.note: The stub's handling verbs moved to Animals on the farm and Evening at the farm.

modules.title: Class in the barn {l'exercice}
modules.goal: You can follow class instructions: read a text, compare two answers, guess what a word means and say it aloud.
modules.situation: Opens with Madame Roux, the maîtresse, handing out paper in the barn for an experiment with milk; closes with a quiz on the farm's words, marked together.
modules.culture_note: The Auvergne takes its name from the Arverni, the Gaulish people of Vercingétorix. In 52 BC he beat Julius Caesar at Gergovie, near today's Clermont-Ferrand, and lost to him at Alésia later that year. Every French child learns his name.

modules.title: Trouble in the dormitory {les bêtises}
modules.goal: You can say that you are angry, ashamed or sorry, complain about someone and forgive them.
modules.situation: Opens when two pupils make fun of Théo and Madame Roux, angry, punishes them; closes with the two ashamed, an apology Théo dares to accept, and nobody jealous of anybody.

modules.title: Théo is ill {la santé}
modules.goal: You can describe symptoms, understand advice and say how you feel.
modules.situation: Opens with Théo ill and weak at breakfast; closes with the nurse's advice: rest, water and his medicine, and he will be better in two days.

modules.title: Evening at the farm {la soirée}
modules.goal: You can ask to borrow something, put things away and play a game of boules.
modules.situation: Opens with the dormitory to tidy before dinner; closes with a game of boules with the farmer under the yard light.
modules.note: Gathers words from the stubs nature-handling-fond, stories-measures-seconde and describing-necessaire, which are retired or changed.

modules.title: Stories in the dark {les histoires qui font peur}
modules.goal: You can tell a scary story in order and say how it ends.
modules.situation: Opens in the dormitory after lights out, when Amélie starts a story about a ghost who guards a treasure in the barn; closes with the monster turned back into an angel, everyone saved, and Théo sure he will have nightmares.

modules.title: Reading · {Le journal de la classe verte}

parts.title: Le journal de la classe verte

reading.genre: news pages written by the pupils: report, interview, weather, health corner, history page
reading.premise: On the last evening, Amélie's class writes a newspaper about its week on Madame Chabrol's farm in the Auvergne. The front page tells the week day by day, from the long bus ride to the afternoon the heat sent everyone into the lake. In an interview, Madame Chabrol says how the farm was run in the past, when her grandfather had forty cows, and how it is run now, with jam and yoghurt sold at the market. The health corner reports that Théo had flu, a sore throat and a fever, that Samir the nurse took care of him, and that another pupil hurt her shoulder playing boules. On the history page Théo tells how Vercingétorix, chief of the Gauls of the Auvergne, beat Julius Caesar at Gergovie in 52 BC, as Madame Roux told the class in the barn. The last page is a list of thank-yous and a promise to come back next year.

He answers from his salon in Lille, teases her that she will come home with a Lyon accent and posts her a box of maroilles, the strong cheese of the north, which Mme Garnier asks her to keep on the window sill. She tells him that Oliver, her English boyfriend, will come over from Bath for a weekend as soon as the site lets her breathe. Words young people use: wesh, meuf, kiffer, relou, and three words the learner knows with a spoken meaning (grave: totally; trop bien: really good; c'est nul: it's rubbish). Short forms in messages: t'inquiète and tkt (don't worry), mdr (the French lol), stp (please). units.title: France through a visitor's eyes {la France vue d'ailleurs}
units.can_do: You can explain French customs to a visitor, compare two countries and concede a point, tell a piece of history from both sides, and say what a writer or a book means to you.

cast: Élodie Renard (29), settled in her flat on the slopes of Fourvière
Oliver Hughes (30), Élodie's boyfriend, a history teacher from Bath in England, in Lyon for his summer holidays; they met on her work placement there, and his French is slow and careful

culture.history: the rivalry between France and England from 1066 to the Entente cordiale; Roman Lyon; Hemingway and the Americans in 1920s Paris; the philosophers
culture.customs: la bise, what a guest brings, coffee at the counter, the order of a meal, strikes and marches, the café philo; verlan

units.sound: Silent h and aspirate h: l'hôte and l'habitude link and take l', while le héros, la hauteur and les hauteurs do not. Then English names said the French way: Oliver, Hemingway, Shakespeare.

modules.title: A guest in France {un invité en France}
modules.goal: You can explain everyday manners to a visitor: how to greet people, what to bring and what not to ask.
modules.situation: Opens with Oliver arriving at Lyon Part-Dieu for the summer and holding out his hand to Mme Garnier, who kisses him on both cheeks and calls him Olivier; closes with Élodie's list for Sunday lunch at Mme Garnier's: bring flowers, say bonjour to everyone in the room, and do not ask what people earn.
modules.culture_note: Friends and family greet each other with la bise, a light kiss on each cheek; a first meeting is usually a handshake. A guest at a French home brings flowers, chocolates or a bottle, and arrives a quarter of an hour after the time given.
modules.spoken_example: On the stairs Léa greets a friend with Wesh, la meuf ! and Oliver asks Élodie what language that was.
modules.note: hôte means both the host and the guest; the lesson teaches it with un invité, which the learner knows.

modules.title: At the counter and at table {au comptoir et à table}
modules.goal: You can order at a café counter, follow a long French meal course by course and raise a glass.
modules.situation: Opens at the bar-tabac on the corner, where Oliver learns that a coffee costs less standing at the counter than sitting on the terrace; closes in a bouchon, one of Lyon's old family restaurants, with the cheese plate arriving before the dessert and everyone looking each other in the eye to clink glasses.
modules.culture_note: A French meal with guests runs in a fixed order: apéritif, starter, main dish, cheese, dessert, coffee. Lyon is known across France for its cooking, and its small traditional restaurants are called bouchons.
modules.spoken_example: Two students at the counter: Cimer, mon reuf. Oliver writes the words on a napkin.

modules.title: Verlan, words turned round ({meuf}, {ouf}, {relou}, {chelou}, {teuf})
modules.goal: Explains verlan, the slang that swaps the syllables of a word: l'envers, the other way round, gives verlan. The learner has met every word here: femme gives meuf, fou gives ouf, lourd gives relou, fête gives teuf, merci gives cimer, énervé gives vénère, frère gives reuf, louche (shady) gives chelou, and flic (a familiar word for a police officer) gives keuf. The swap is made by ear, so the spelling changes and a last vowel often drops. Verlan is young people's speech among friends; meuf, ouf and relou are now heard from adults too. Keuf is said about the police, never to them. Léa explains it to Oliver over a coffee, and he tries it on his own name. The learner recognises these words and is never asked to produce them.

modules.title: Best enemies {les meilleurs ennemis}
modules.goal: You can tell a piece of shared history from both sides and tease someone about it without offending.
modules.situation: Opens on the balcony of Élodie's flat, with Oliver, who teaches history, listing England's victories over France and Élodie answering with France's; closes with both agreeing that the two countries have been allies for more than a century, and that neither will ever admit the other cooks better.
modules.culture_note: France and England fought each other for centuries, from the Hundred Years' War to Waterloo in 1815, and have been allies since the Entente cordiale of 1904. The teasing goes on: the French call the English les rosbifs, and the English call the French frogs.

modules.title: Strikes and paperwork {grèves et papiers}
modules.goal: You can explain why people are protesting, compare how two countries do things and concede a point.
modules.situation: Opens with Oliver's train to Paris cancelled by a strike and a march passing under the window; closes with Élodie conceding that French paperwork is painful, while the English, she says, queue for everything without a word.
modules.culture_note: Strikes and street marches are an ordinary part of public life in France, and the right to strike is written into the constitution. Most marches are announced in advance and follow an agreed route.

modules.title: A café philo with Odile {le café philo}
modules.goal: You can say what a thinker claimed, quote a line and say whether you find it convincing.
modules.situation: Opens in the back room of Le Familia, where Odile, who taught philosophy for forty years, runs a café philo once a month and puts one of her old exam questions to the room: can we be free and afraid at once?; closes with Oliver quoting Descartes in careful French, Je pense, donc je suis, and Odile asking him to justify it.
modules.culture_note: A café philo is a public discussion of one philosophical question, open to anyone, usually in a café; the first was held in Paris in 1992. Descartes, Voltaire, Rousseau, Sartre, Beauvoir and Camus are names most French adults met in their last year of school.

modules.title: Roman Lyon {Lugdunum}
modules.goal: You can show someone round an ancient site: what stood where, who built it and what is left.
modules.situation: Opens at the top of Fourvière hill, above Élodie's new flat, in the Roman theatre built two thousand years ago; closes with Oliver saying that his town, Bath, has Roman baths too, and Élodie answering that Lyon had an emperor: Claudius was born here.
modules.culture_note: The Romans founded Lyon in 43 BC as Lugdunum, and it became the capital of Roman Gaul. Their theatre on Fourvière hill, begun about 15 BC, is still used for concerts every summer.

modules.title: A weekend in Paris with Hemingway {Paris est une fête}
modules.goal: You can talk about a writer's life and a book: when it was written, what it tells and why people still read it.
modules.situation: Opens in front of Shakespeare and Company, the English-language bookshop across the river from Notre-Dame, where Oliver buys A Moveable Feast and Élodie its French translation, Paris est une fête; closes on a café terrace in Montparnasse, each reading the same chapter in their own language.
modules.culture_note: Ernest Hemingway lived in Paris from the end of 1921 and wrote about those years in A Moveable Feast, published in 1964, after his death. The French know the book as Paris est une fête.

reading.genre: a Sunday lunch told in dialogue, then an explanatory text; in two parts
reading.premise: Part 1, in which a character learns alongside the reader: Mme Garnier invites Élodie and Oliver to Sunday lunch and tests the English history teacher between courses. He gives her Agincourt and Waterloo; she gives him William of Normandy, who took England in 1066, and Joan of Arc. Léa keeps the score on a napkin. They agree on the Entente cordiale of 1904 and on the tunnel under the Channel, disagree on whether cheese comes before or after dessert, and end with Mme Garnier teaching Oliver to say grenouille while he teaches her to say squirrel. Part 2, exposition: why so many American writers lived in Paris in the 1920s. After the First World War a dollar bought a great deal in France, and a young reporter named Ernest Hemingway arrived in December 1921 with his wife Hadley. The text follows him from the flat on the rue du Cardinal-Lemoine to Gertrude Stein's salon and to Sylvia Beach's bookshop, Shakespeare and Company, which lent him the books he could not afford. It ends with the memoir he wrote about those years, published in 1964, after his death: A Moveable Feast, which the French read as Paris est une fête.
reading.questions: in part 1, who wins each round and which points the two agree on; in part 2, why American writers came to Paris, where Hemingway lived and read, and what the memoir tells
